---
title: "Web Workflow"
---

> ⚠️ **Prerequisite**  
> You need an active workspace and application.  
> → Start with [Create Your First Feature](/docs/build/quick-start)

The web workflow is the dashboard-first way to use Build. It is useful when multiple teammates need visibility into what was requested, what Revolte generated, and where the pull request is in the review process.

## When to use the web workflow

Use the dashboard when:

- Product, design, QA, or operations teammates need visibility
- You are starting from the workspace instead of a local checkout
- You want to review build history across applications
- You need a guided workflow for less terminal-heavy users
- You want the generated pull request linked from the application context

## How it works

<Steps>
  <Step title="Open Build">
    Select the workspace, project, and application. Then open the Build area for that application.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Submit a requirement">
    Describe the feature or fix in plain language, including expected behavior and validation criteria.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Track progress">
    Watch Revolte move through analysis, planning, implementation, and validation.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Open the pull request">
    Use the generated pull request link to inspect the diff, tests, and summary.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Merge or request changes">
    Approve the output when it is ready, or refine the request if the implementation needs adjustment.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Example request

```txt
Create an admin-only page for viewing failed deployments. Include filters by environment and status, show the last failed deployment time, and add tests for access control.
```

This request is strong because it names:

- The user role
- The page behavior
- The fields to display
- The filters to support
- The validation requirement

## CLI vs web

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Use CLI when">
    - You are actively editing or testing locally.
    - The task depends on local command output.
    - You want terminal-first approval of actions.
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="Use Web when">
    - You want dashboard visibility.
    - Non-developer teammates need to follow progress.
    - You are reviewing builds across applications.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Review from the dashboard

The dashboard should help you answer:

- What requirement started this build?
- What state is the build in?
- Was validation completed?
- Where is the generated pull request?
- Does the output need another iteration?

## Best practices

- Put acceptance criteria directly in the requirement.
- Keep the first request small enough to review.
- Link the build to the relevant issue or product context when available.
- Open the pull request before merging, even when validation passes.
